About this game

The full-map WWII grand-strategy board game, with the usability of a modern digital board game.

Rules fidelity

Full Global 1940, by the book

Both 1940 boards are joined into one map, with every rule in: strategic bombing, amphibious assault, scramble, submarines, kamikaze, canals, convoys, capital capture and the split UK economy. The game only offers legal moves, and it was built from a citation-indexed transcription of the official rulebooks.

Engine

Deterministic engine, dice you can check

The same state, move and seed always produce byte-identical output. Every game can be replayed from its opening position plus an append-only action log. Dice are committed cryptographically before the result is known, so any player can audit any roll.

Async play

Nobody waits on an absent opponent

Defenders pre-set Defense Profiles (casualty order, scrambles, kamikaze), so the attacker never stalls. Players who are online can use Live Defense Mode to take over their own battles in real time. If they disconnect, their profile takes back over.

Command

Plan a whole offensive in a few clicks

Shift-click units from several territories into one battle group and right-click a target to attack with all of them. Before you commit, a summary screen shows every battle you're starting next to what's defending it. Revert Phase undoes a phase safely, and a dice log tracks every roll.

Modes

Fog of War, espionage and alternate wars

An animated WebGL fog hides everything your forces can't see, with recon planes and spies to scout through it. There are six scenarios, including scrambled-team and five-power setups, plus Infinity War, a six-gem power mode. Research & Development, National Objectives, special units and abilities, and a dozen house rules can each be switched on per game.

Multiplayer

Lobbies, spectators, turn alerts

You can claim nations, share seats, see who's online and resume anything in progress. Spectators follow games live, including a mirrored battle board, and players get an email when it's their turn. The art is real 1940s poster work from public archives, set to an original score.

How it was built

One developer, AI coding tools, and a fixed budget. First commit to friends playing in under six months.

Ironclad began with one question: could one person working with AI coding tools ship a faithful, production-grade version of the most rules-heavy WWII board game there is? The first commit landed in May 2026, and a closed group of friends was playing real games by summer.

<6 moConcept to production
548Commits
~150kLines of TypeScript / JS
~3,700Automated tests
69Citation-indexed rules chunks
v0.79Versioned engine releases

Scoping & architecture

Breaking a huge ruleset into parts

I split two rulebooks of interlocking, multi-variable rules into self-contained domains: combat, movement, politics, economy and setup. Then I designed a modular architecture around them, with shared types, a pure rules engine, an authoritative server and a thin client. I picked the hosting environment and set a strict MVP-versus-v1 roadmap, with out-of-scope features written down so they stayed out.

Resource-constrained AI prototyping

Shipping under hard usage caps

All of it was built with LLM developer tools under strict per-session and weekly usage budgets. That forced hard prioritization: core rules logic and correctness came first, and non-essential features waited. The result was a production-ready app in under six months, not a demo.

Agile execution

A living backlog, shipped continuously

I kept a running backlog of user stories and audit findings and worked through it in short, testable slices. That covered rules bugs, state-management edge cases (replay, reconnects, mid-combat state) and async notification loops such as turn-alert emails. Every rule-affecting change got a versioned engine release and a migration, so saved games keep loading.

User-centric feedback loops

A closed beta that steers the roadmap

I recruited a closed beta group to drive continuous discovery. Their reports go straight into the backlog, and fixes, UX changes and balance tweaks usually ship within days, logged in an in-app changelog. Battle groups, summary screens, Revert Phase and Live Defense Mode were all built and refined this way.

What you need

It runs in the browser. There is nothing to install and nothing to pay.

To play
A current version of Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari. It's best on a laptop and playable on a phone held in landscape. You can add it to your home screen to run it as an app.
To join
An invitation. New accounts are approved by the owner, then open the app.
Built with
React & TypeScript · Leaflet tiled map with a WebGL fog layer · Node & Fastify · PostgreSQL (snapshots + append-only action log) · WebSockets · a standalone deterministic rules engine · Docker on Railway.

Ironclad is a fan-made digital adaptation of Axis & Allies: Global 1940, built for private play among friends. It is not affiliated with, licensed by, or endorsed by Hasbro, Avalon Hill or Wizards of the Coast, and has no connection to Steam or Valve. All rulebook text is transcribed for reference only.
